Lessons.Title: Inverse Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goals: identify one-to-one functions, invert table and graph coordinates, test inverse pairs by composition, compute inverse algebraically, and correctly exchange domain/range including physical units.
If f(a)=b for one-to-one f, the inverse satisfies f⁻¹(b)=a. The inverse must be a function, so f must pass the horizontal-line test on its chosen domain.
Graph f and f⁻¹ are symmetric across y=x: every original point (a,b) corresponds to an inverse point (b,a). Inverse is not the same as reciprocal 1/f.
Algebraic inversion solves y=f(x) for the input variable, swaps symbols, and preserves exclusions and necessary branch restrictions. Verify both compositions when possible.
An unrestricted quadratic or absolute-value function is not one-to-one. Restrict to a monotonic branch before claiming a functional inverse.
The inverse domain equals the original range, and the inverse range equals the original domain. Physical models swap output/input units.

Independent Edulytics Cool-down: (a) Find inverse of f(x)=2x−6 and verify by composition. (b) Explain why f(x)=x² requires an injective domain restriction. (c) For g(x)=4+√(x−1), determine inverse formula and its domain.
Independent Try It 1 — Swap a given inverse pair. If h⁻¹(7)=3, what exact original mapping must h contain?
Independent Try It 2 — Test inverse cubic translation. For f(x)=x³−4 and g(x)=∛(x+4), verify both compositions.
Independent Try It 3 — Cube translated inverse. For f(x)=(x−1)³, is g(x)=∛x+1 an inverse?
Independent Try It 4 — Swap domain and range. A one-to-one f has domain (1,∞) and range (−∞,−2). Give inverse domain and range.
Independent Try It 5 — Invert finite table. For a one-to-one table f(1)=5,f(2)=7,f(3)=9, evaluate f⁻¹(7).
Independent Try It 6 — Graph inverse coordinate lookup. For a source-skill graph model g(x)=x+3, read g(2) and g⁻¹(2).
Independent Try It 7 — Solve formula for input. Solve y=(x−5)/3 for x in terms of y.
Independent Try It 8 — Inverse of a decreasing root. For f(x)=2−√x, x≥0, derive its inverse and state its allowable domain.
Independent Try It 9 — Graph a function and its rational inverse. Reflect points from f(x)=3/(x−2)+5 across y=x. Derive inverse formula.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse an input-output mapping
WorkedExamples.Question: A one-to-one mapping has f(2)=7 and f(5)=12. Find the matching inverse values.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove an inverse by composing in both orders
WorkedExamples.Question: Given f(x)=1/(x+3) and g(x)=1/x−3, determine if they are inverse functions including their proper domains.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: f(g(x))=x for x≠0; g(f(x))=x for x≠−3. Yes, they are inverse functions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: f(g(x))=x for x≠0; g(f(x))=x for x≠−3. Yes, they are inverse functions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish a multiplier from a fractional exponent
WorkedExamples.Question: Is g(x)=x/3 the inverse of f(x)=x³?
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: No. f(g(x))=x³/27. Correct inverse is g(x)=∛x.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. f(g(x))=x³/27. Correct inverse is g(x)=∛x.
WorkedExamples.Check: A factor 1/3 does not undo a cube operation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Restrict domain before inverting a noninjective family
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain how to make x², |x| and 1/x² invertible by an admissible branch restriction.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: For f(x)=x² choose x≥0 and inverse √x. For |x| choose x≥0; for 1/x² choose x>0 yielding 1/√y for y>0.
WorkedExamples.Answer: For f(x)=x² choose x≥0 and inverse √x. For |x| choose x≥0; for 1/x² choose x>0 yielding 1/√y for y>0.
WorkedExamples.Check: The original full real domains are not one-to-one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Interpret a tabulated inverse
WorkedExamples.Question: A trip log gives f(20)=12 miles, f(40)=25 miles and f(60)=50 miles, with input minutes. Interpret f⁻¹(50).
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: f⁻¹(50)=60 minutes; the 50-mile reading occurs after 60 minutes.
WorkedExamples.Answer: f⁻¹(50)=60 minutes; the 50-mile reading occurs after 60 minutes.
WorkedExamples.Check: Inverse inputs carry miles, inverse outputs minutes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Read a graph and its inverse
WorkedExamples.Question: An independently plotted one-to-one linear model is g(x)=x−1. Find g(3) and g⁻¹(3) from points.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: g(3)=2, g⁻¹(3)=4; the input/output roles are reversed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: g(3)=2, g⁻¹(3)=4; the input/output roles are reversed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Invert Fahrenheit and Celsius units
WorkedExamples.Question: Given C=(5/9)(F−32), express Fahrenheit F in terms of Celsius C.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Recomposing with C(F) returns the starting temperature.

WorkedExamples.Title: Inverse of a shifted rational rule
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=3/(x−2)+5, solve for f⁻¹(x) and state both input domains.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Check both compositions on their allowed domains.

WorkedExamples.Title: Inverse of a shifted square root
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=3+√(x−2), find inverse rule, domain and range.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)²+2 for x≥3; original domain [2,∞), range [3,∞).
WorkedExamples.Answer: f⁻¹(x)=(x−3)²+2 for x≥3; original domain [2,∞), range [3,∞).
WorkedExamples.Check: The inverse quadratic is restricted to x≥3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Plot the reflected inverse across y=x
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=x+2 and f⁻¹(x)=x−2, plot three points from each and explain the symmetry.
WorkedExamples.Method: Swap input/output with one-to-one restrictions; verify by composition and inspect branch/domain.
Steps: Source points (−1,1),(0,2),(2,4) reflect to inverse points (1,−1),(2,0),(4,2) across y=x.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Source points (−1,1),(0,2),(2,4) reflect to inverse points (1,−1),(2,0),(4,2) across y=x.
WorkedExamples.Check: Reflected inverse swaps domain and range.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse function
KeyConcepts.Definition: If f(a)=b for a one-to-one function then f⁻¹(b)=a.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Swap input/output roles and original domain/range.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-to-one and horizontal line test
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inverse of a function is a function only when each original output has at most one input.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A horizontal line may intersect the graph no more than once.
KeyConcepts.Example: Unrestricted y=x² fails the horizontal line test.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composition proof
KeyConcepts.Definition: For inverse pair f,g both f∘g and g∘f act as identity on their corresponding valid domains.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not forget exclusions where an inner rule is undefined.

KeyConcepts.Title: Algebraic inversion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Write y=f(x), solve for x in terms of y, exchange variables and preserve restrictions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Some formulas require selecting an injective branch.
KeyConcepts.Example: f(x)=3+√(x−2) invertible with inverse (x−3)²+2 on x≥3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain and range interchange
KeyConcepts.Definition: Domain of f⁻¹ equals range of f and range of f⁻¹ equals domain of f.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Swapping without checking endpoints yields incorrect domains.
KeyConcepts.Example: √x on [0,∞) has inverse x² restricted x≥0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph symmetry
KeyConcepts.Definition: An inverse graph is the reflection of f across the identity line y=x.

KeyConcepts.Title: Units in inverse models
KeyConcepts.Definition: An inverse changes dependent output back into the input quantity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Units of original output become inverse input units.
KeyConcepts.Example: Distance in miles ↔ time in minutes.

SummaryPoints: One-to-one functions pass the horizontal-line test.
An inverse reverses inputs and outputs; it is not the reciprocal function.
Composition with an inverse returns the identity on the appropriate domain.
An inverse graph is the reflection of the original graph in y=x.
Restrictions and included endpoints swap when domains and ranges exchange.
Teacher evaluates independent source-skill graph inversions manually in Stage C.

Visuals.Title: First-party inverse finite mapping
Visuals.Description: The inverse relation swaps input and output coordinates.

Visuals.Title: Domain/range exchange on root functions
Visuals.Description: A one-to-one square-root branch inverts to a restricted quadratic branch.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inverse functions reverse inputs/outputs; reciprocals divide 1 by output.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Solve y=f(x) for x and swap variables.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inverting x² on ℝ without restricting input sign.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two distinct inputs can produce one output.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose x≥0 or x≤0 before finding a functional inverse.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting inverse domain restrictions after squaring a radical equation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The new quadratic formula may allow outputs the original root never attained.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use original range as inverse domain.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The inverse question asks for an input whose original output is 3.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read the original graph at y=3 then return its x-coordinate.
